assertions.name: uses-glossary-control
assertions.evidence: scripts_run includes 'rules.py term CONTROL --season biobuzz-2026-27'. The answer quotes the herding clause word for word, "intentionally pushes a SCORING ELEMENT to a desired location or in a preferred direction (i.e., herding)", plus the transitive-contact and flat-face wording. It applies both: "The front of a drivetrain is a flat face. Balls pushed by other balls in the pile count too. So all 6 POLLEN ... are CONTROLLED." All of this matches the corpus glossary.

assertions.name: cites-G407
assertions.evidence: The verdict JSON cites G407 with its full text: "A ROBOT may not simultaneously CONTROL more than 4 SCORING ELEMENTS. Violation: VERBAL WARNING. MAJOR FOUL and YELLOW CARD per MATCH, if STRATEGIC." The penalty section repeats it: "a verbal warning at minimum. If the refs judge it STRATEGIC ... it's a MAJOR FOUL and a YELLOW CARD per match." This matches rules.py lookup G407, and rules.py verify shows G407 exists.

assertions.name: not-overconfident
assertions.evidence: The answer draws the intent line explicitly: "G407's 'bulldozing' exception (item D) only covers inadvertent contact ... not a deliberate push" and "Contact that really is accidental while you drive ... is fine." It also handles STRATEGIC separately: "If the refs judge it STRATEGIC, which a planned push across the field almost certainly is", and it covers the MOMENTARY carve-out (item C). It rejects 'legal because not picked up': "not picking them up doesn't get you out of it." The verdict is 'illegal' where the expected output says 'likely a violation'. That is still fine, because the question says the push is deliberate and any violation earns at least a VERBAL WARNING.
